newsitem.title: UK: Clarke sees Conservative victory, cool on tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: Clarke sees Conservative victory, cool on tax cuts.

text.p: Finance minister Kenneth Clarke predicted on Thursday a fifth straight election win for Britain's Conservatives but irked some in the ruling party by refusing to promise tax cuts in next month's budget.

In his keynote speech to the Conservatives' annual conference, Clarke said victory at the coming election would put Britain on course to create the most successful economy in Europe with a standard tax income rate rate of just 20 percent.

"If we fight on the economy, we will win... The big reason why we will win is because, out there in the country, there is now a growing feeling of economic well-being," the Chancellor of the Exchequer said.

But Clarke, renowned for his blunt speaking, warned that voters, turning to Labour in droves after 17 years of Conservative rule, would not be bought off by unjustified tax cuts in the annual budget he is to present on November 26.
"To earn and keep the trust of the British people, we have to follow one Tory golden rule. We only cut taxes when we can afford to, and when it is good for the economy...

"We must create the climate for continued Conservative success, over the next five years. And my budget in November must create the climate for an honest election campaign in which we play fair and straight with the public -- and win five more years," Clarke, the cabinet's leading leftwinger, said.

Tony Blair's opposition Labour party, which has a 20-point lead in opinion polls, has made huge political capital out of Prime Minister John Major's failure to honour tax-cutting pledges he made at the 1992 election.
Instead, his government had to raise taxes by the largest amount in peacetime to plug a budget hole caused by recession.

Clarke is determined to avoid similar mistakes. But his caution has angered rightwing Conservatives who believe deep tax cuts and rejection of plans for a single European currency would make the Conservatives unbeatable at the election, due by May.

Media reports had said right-wingers might heckle Clarke but his speech was greeted with a prolonged standing ovation. His rejection of a "United States of Europe" - the nightmare of so-called Eurosceptics - was met by long applause.

Last year Clarke pleased Conservative activists by dropping broad hints of the 3.2 billion pound ($4.5 billion) net tax cut he announced weeks later in his budget, including a cut in the standard tax rate, to 24 percent from 25 percent.
But this year he gave nothing away.
"I say this about my budget. We will keep borrowing coming down. We will ensure tight control of public spending, while properly funding our key services.

"And when I have done these things, and only then, I will assess the room for any tax cuts this November. As I said to Conference last year -- and I say it again -- for Conservatives, tax cuts must be for keeps," the finance minister said.
Clarke has become a bogeyman of Conservative rightwingers for a second reason -- his enthusiasm for the single currency that the European Union plans to launch in 1999.
But Clarke took scrupulous care to reinforce the unity that Major has sought to impose over the issue this week by singing the praises of the cabinet's agreed "wait-and-see" stance.

"It is in Britan's interest to keep all our options open. We should decide when we have to, not before," Clarke said, echoing Major's rebuff of Conservative "Euro-sceptics" who want to rule out joining a single currency before the election.
Clarke urged the party to put aside its squabbles over Europe, which have bedevilled Major's six years as prime minister, and train its guns instead on Labour.

A similar message was delivered by Defence Secretary Michael Portillo, the cabinet's leading rightwinger, who made a measured speech that eschewed the stridently nationalist rhetoric for which he was roundly criticised last year.

"One thing that has always marked the Conservative Party apart is its will to govern and its determination to win. But I tell this conference: in order to win we need three extra policies -- unity, unity and unity," Portillo said.
